newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Britannia rules the waves, but not for long.
newsitem.headline: Britannia rules the waves, but not for long.

text.p: The most glamorous guest at ceremonies marking Hong Kong's June 30 handover to China is likely to be an elegant 44-year-old royal lady.
Well-travelled but expensive to maintain, her life is nearly over.
Her name is Britannia, the British royal yacht, which steams into Hong Kong harbour on Monday on the penultimate leg of her last offical voyage.

Britannia's arrival complete with a crew of 236, a Royal Marine band and acres of polished brass fittings will mean the stage is set for an end-of-empire bash expected to be watched by 100 million television viewers around the world.
Launched in 1953 as a floating palace for Britain's royal family, Britannia has been a potent symbol of the nation's naval tradition.
The ship ends her million-mile odyssey later this year when she returns to Britain to be decommissioned, a victim of age and the country's growing disillusion with monarchy.
As a prop for the elaborately scripted handover drama, Britannia threatens to upstage Hong Kong's glittering new waterfront convention centre, where the actual ceremony will take place.

Prince Charles will use the 412-foot, three-masted yacht as his base for the festivities. The ship, lying at anchor in Hong Kong harbour just off the convention centre, is to be the stage for a number of dinners, parties and high-level meetings.
Shortly after the formal handover at midnight on June 30 Prince Charles and last colonial Governor Chris Patten will leave together, sailing off into the darkness aboard Britannia.
That the ship's last official voyage should coincide with Hong Kong's return to China after a colonial interlude of more than 150 years is rich with symbolism and significance.

Britannia's working life has virtually spanned the reign of Queen Elizabeth II, who came to the throne in 1952. That Britain would always have a monarch and a Hong Kong were beyond doubt when the ship was launched. Times have changed.

The intervening 44 years have seen Britain's status as a world power decline. Hong Kong's 1997 return to China was agreed by negotiation in 1984. Meanwhile, British public support for the monarchy has declined sharply.

With her large crew and an antiquated steam plant originally lifted from a British submarine in 1943, Britannia has been costing British taxpayers about eight million pounds ($13 million) a year to operate.

Public griping about the monarchy's perceived irrelevance to modern Britain and complaints about the royal family's lavish, subsidised life-style have convinced many that Britannia is a luxury the country cannot afford.
Then-defence minister Michael Portillo said in January that a new $100 million yacht would be commissioned to replace Britannia.
A public opinion poll at the time said 72 per cent of Britons disapproved of the government paying for the new yacht.
Then in opposition, the Labour Party declared that it would not pay for a new yacht if it came to power. It later swept to victory in the May 1 general election.
